name: Sara Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain flood-warning software, checking gauge readings against the warning screen and fixing the code when they disagree; I like turning a vague alert into something residents can use. I use AI every day for draft tests, but a field worker's photograph can overturn a neat result. My partner drives trains, and we have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the assistant can sort routine rain-gauge alerts, but I want a person to check the gauge before a warning goes out. I use AI every day to draft tests for our flood-warning software, then compare them with the recorded water levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the change stays small, I expect my pay and role to hold. I earn well for my developer work, my partner drives trains on steady hours, we have roughly ten months of expenses saved, and there are many software employers nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking the morning gauge feed and the warning page before each release. In the first year I'd continue using AI only on sample readings, and add 250 to savings each pay period while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household. I still get a jolt when a warning page says a gauge is fine and the river is clearly rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the feed and the field disagree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A gauge once froze on the same number for six hours. The assistant called the readings stable, but a field worker sent us a photograph of water over the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about warnings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask our children to treat a flood warning as a reason to check the local instructions, not to stand at the water and see for themselves. Software can help, but it must be honest about missing readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI writing code, checking data and answering residents could make our warning team smaller. We need to count false-safe messages alongside the hours saved before deciding who remains on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be kept for the warning rules, but a smaller team could also cut me. Our savings let us search, yet the idea of field workers relying on an unchecked AI answer bothers me as much as the job risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run an eight-week trial on old gauge failures, counting false-safe warnings and the minutes staff spend checking each one. If the trial improves both, I'd learn the new review process; in the first year I'd join the staff association's meeting to ask for a written staffing and paid-training plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own post, but ready to test the claim properly. I don't want a good score hiding a dangerous missed alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which test would you insist on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The frozen-gauge case must be in that trial. If the tool calls six hours of identical readings safe, we need to see that failure before the public sees a green map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose evidence belongs at the staff meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our association includes field staff, not only developers. I'd ask the group to bring their photographs and error reports into the meeting. A tidy code test is not a field check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches our code and warning decisions before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A flood warning needs an accountable person when a gauge fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the company could cut much of our development work, including my post, even if I use AI daily. Ten months saved and my partner's train wage buy time, but I would still lie awake if many local firms stopped hiring developers at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep a clean record of the frozen-gauge fix without resident details and ask three local firms about paid field-data review posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to real vacancies whose wage with my partner's pay covers mortgage and school costs; if none meet that test, I'd keep looking for paid work while using savings, and ask the association to press for notice and funded training before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A cushion is helpful. A whole group of software employers can stop hiring developers at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would field work be safe after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Field-data review would mean checking sensor readings against reports from people on the ground. Robots may take more hands-on gauge checks around 2031, so I'd ask firms for real duties and paid hours rather than call it safe for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner about savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner exactly what the ten months cover. We would not promise our children a house move or a new school based on a phone call about a possible post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us test warning systems across several wet seasons. Robots follow around 2034, but thinking AI changes the code and decisions first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build paid work checking field evidence against generated warnings, if employers still want people in that role. My current developer post might shrink by 2031, so I would not buy training merely because a job title sounds reassuring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our field manager to let me shadow one gauge inspection each quarter if my software manager releases the time. I'd take a safety course only if my firm funds it and offers paid field-review duties; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for those posts only if vacancies remain and household wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own wage, though five years give me time to test a route. I can watch what the field actually needs before resigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at an inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At an inspection I would check how the worker knows a gauge has frozen, then compare the field note with our display. I would not touch flood gauges without training and authorisation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make field duties real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask if the field duties mean paid hours on a written rota. If not, I'd keep my software role and ask the association to press for a real training path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to record how real floods differ from a screen. Thinking AI reaches warning code in 2036; robots come around 2039 for hands-on gauge work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be doing paid field review or another software job. Our higher pay, my partner's steady train wage and ten-month cushion make the next few years secure, but I cannot promise which role still pays after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep documenting frozen-gauge errors without resident details and make the warning page clearer about missing readings. We'd add 250 to savings each pay period while both wages hold, and join the staff association each year to request paid-role numbers; after 2036 I'd change jobs only for a signed offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our present income. A decade lets us act from error records and paid offers, not a frightening headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful error record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would show the six-hour frozen reading, the field photograph and the warning we corrected. I want the next developer to remember the gauge failure. A flat flood-gauge line can still mean rising water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about AI work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask whether their future jobs will use AI. I'd tell them to learn the work behind the screen and check real course costs when they are ready; I cannot decide their jobs for them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because warning code jobs could shrink across many firms at once. Notice before cuts, funded field training and paid review posts with clear responsibility would help us plan without guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who calls residents after a false safe message. Someone must own a false flood-warning correction, even if a machine drew the green map; otherwise residents may trust it again.

headlineQuote: Someone must own a false flood-warning correction, even if a machine drew the green map; otherwise residents may trust it again.
portrait: Sara, **43**, is an experienced flood-warning developer with a bachelor's degree who checks gauge feeds against field reports.
Her **higher pay**, partner's train wage, ten-month cushion and many nearby software firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **daily** but caught a frozen gauge that made rising water look stable.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about staffing; fast 2028 AGI alarms her about broad coding losses.
With more time, she pursues **paid field review**, funded training and staff-group requests, moving only for bill-covering signed wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove warning-code jobs across firms despite her strong cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice before cuts**, funded field training and accountable paid review posts would help.
